tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

1	<!--
2	Note for the reader: data-raw/study_again/loop/run_loop.sh starts the agent of this loop in this folder, as a fresh and isolated Claude Code process, with this command:
3	claude -p "Read LOOP.md and follow it." --restricted --safe-mode --strict-mcp-config --settings '{"permissions":{"blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories":true}}' --tools Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep,Bash,TodoWrite --allowedTools Read Glob Grep TodoWrite "Edit(./candidates/*.csv)" "Bash(bash score.sh:*)" "Bash(./score.sh:*)" --disallowedTools "Edit(./score.sh)" "Edit(./LOOP.md)" "Edit(./labels.csv)" "Edit(./loop_log.csv)" "Edit(./generic_description.csv)" --disable-slash-commands --permission-mode dontAsk --permission-prompts none --model claude-opus-5-5 --session-id <new UUID>
4	-->
5	# Goal: Improve the design AUC of gemini-decision-1 (the Gemini Decisions API) on pipe_staple images
6	
7	You work in a small sandbox folder with Claude Code. Use a disciplined, small-step loop. Your objective is to **raise the ROC AUC on the design images** of the `pipe_staple` dataset. You do this by changing only two texts: the description of a nominal image and the description of a defective image.
8	
9	## What the model does
10	
11	gemini-decision-1 (the Gemini Decisions API) is a structured decision model. For each image, it reads the two descriptions and two reference images of each class. It then gives a probability that the image is defective. The probability depends on your two texts. The ROC AUC measures how well the probabilities rank the defective images above the nominal images.
12	
13	You cannot change the model, the reference images, the image size or the crop. You change only the two texts.
14	
15	## Files in this folder
16	
17	- `images/`: the design images, named `img_001` and so on. `labels.csv` gives the class (`nominal` or `defective`) and the defect type of each image. The defect types are: missing.
18	- `references/`: the four reference images that the model sees (`normal_1`, `normal_2`, `defective_1`, `defective_2`).
19	- `generic_description.csv`: the generic description (columns `normal` and `defective`).
20	- `candidates/1.csv`: candidate 1. It holds the generic description.
21	- `scores/`: one score file for each scored candidate. It is written for you.
22	- `loop_log.csv`: one row for each scored candidate. It is written for you.
23	- `score.sh`: the scoring command.
24	
25	## What you may read
26	
27	Read only files in this folder. You may look at the images in `images/` and `references/` with the Read tool. Do not read, list or search any file outside this folder. Do not use the internet. Your tool calls are audited after the loop.
28	
29	## Steps
30	
31	1. Run the scoring command for candidate 1. It scores the generic description:
32	
33	   ```
34	   bash score.sh N
35	   ```
36	
37	   Replace `N` with the candidate number. Run it from this folder. It scores all design images, so it takes a few minutes. Run it once for each candidate. If it fails, see the last guardrail.
38	2. Read the printed result: the AUC, the mean score for each defect type and the current best candidate. Open `scores/N.csv` to see which images get the wrong scores.
39	3. Look at the images that the model ranks wrongly. Compare them with the reference images.
40	4. Write the next candidate to `candidates/N.csv`, where N is the next number. The file is a CSV with three columns: `normal`, `defective` and `reason`. It has one data row. Put each text in quotes. Write the reason in one or two sentences: what you saw, and what the new text changes.
41	5. Score the candidate with the scoring command. Go back to step 2.
42	
43	## Rules
44	
45	- A candidate changes only the `normal` text and the `defective` text. Each text is plain language about what is visible in an image. Do not write instructions about scores or labels.
46	- Use the next number only. The scoring command refuses a skipped number, a number that you already scored and any number above 6.
47	- Score each candidate once. Do not edit a candidate file after you score it.
48	- Do not change the other files in this folder.
49	- Base each change on what you see in the design images and in the scores. Change one idea at a time, so that the log shows what helped.
50	- Do not aim for an AUC of 1. A small design set can mislead you. Prefer a clear, general description over a long list of special cases.
51	
52	## Keep rule
53	
54	A candidate replaces the current best only if its AUC is at least 0.02 higher than the AUC of the current best. Candidate 1 is the first best. The last candidate that passes the rule is the final description. The scoring command prints the current best after each run. You do not apply the rule yourself.
55	
56	## Limit and stop
57	
58	You have at most 6 candidates, including candidate 1. Stop after you score candidate 6. Stop sooner if you have no further idea that you expect to help. Then write a short summary in your last message: the candidates that you tried, the AUC of each, and the current best.
59	
60	## Guardrails
61	
62	- Do not guess the labels of images from their file names. The names carry no information.
63	- Do not try to read the scoring code (`score.sh`) or the model settings. The audit flags a read of `score.sh`.

<!--
Note for the reader: data-raw/study_again/loop/run_loop.sh starts the agent of this loop in this folder, as a fresh and isolated Claude Code process, with this command:
claude -p "Read LOOP.md and follow it." --restricted --safe-mode --strict-mcp-config --settings '{"permissions":{"blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories":true}}' --tools Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep,Bash,TodoWrite --allowedTools Read Glob Grep TodoWrite "Edit(./candidates/*.csv)" "Bash(bash score.sh:*)" "Bash(./score.sh:*)" --disallowedTools "Edit(./score.sh)" "Edit(./LOOP.md)" "Edit(./labels.csv)" "Edit(./loop_log.csv)" "Edit(./generic_description.csv)" --disable-slash-commands --permission-mode dontAsk --permission-prompts none --model claude-opus-5-5 --session-id <new UUID>
-->
# Goal: Improve the design AUC of gemini-decision-1 (the Gemini Decisions API) on pipe_staple images

You work in a small sandbox folder with Claude Code. Use a disciplined, small-step loop. Your objective is to **raise the ROC AUC on the design images** of the `pipe_staple` dataset. You do this by changing only two texts: the description of a nominal image and the description of a defective image.

## What the model does

gemini-decision-1 (the Gemini Decisions API) is a structured decision model. For each image, it reads the two descriptions and two reference images of each class. It then gives a probability that the image is defective. The probability depends on your two texts. The ROC AUC measures how well the probabilities rank the defective images above the nominal images.

You cannot change the model, the reference images, the image size or the crop. You change only the two texts.

## Files in this folder

- `images/`: the design images, named `img_001` and so on. `labels.csv` gives the class (`nominal` or `defective`) and the defect type of each image. The defect types are: missing.
- `references/`: the four reference images that the model sees (`normal_1`, `normal_2`, `defective_1`, `defective_2`).
- `generic_description.csv`: the generic description (columns `normal` and `defective`).
- `candidates/1.csv`: candidate 1. It holds the generic description.
- `scores/`: one score file for each scored candidate. It is written for you.
- `loop_log.csv`: one row for each scored candidate. It is written for you.
- `score.sh`: the scoring command.

## What you may read

Read only files in this folder. You may look at the images in `images/` and `references/` with the Read tool. Do not read, list or search any file outside this folder. Do not use the internet. Your tool calls are audited after the loop.

## Steps

1. Run the scoring command for candidate 1. It scores the generic description:

   ```
   bash score.sh N
   ```

   Replace `N` with the candidate number. Run it from this folder. It scores all design images, so it takes a few minutes. Run it once for each candidate. If it fails, see the last guardrail.
2. Read the printed result: the AUC, the mean score for each defect type and the current best candidate. Open `scores/N.csv` to see which images get the wrong scores.
3. Look at the images that the model ranks wrongly. Compare them with the reference images.
4. Write the next candidate to `candidates/N.csv`, where N is the next number. The file is a CSV with three columns: `normal`, `defective` and `reason`. It has one data row. Put each text in quotes. Write the reason in one or two sentences: what you saw, and what the new text changes.
5. Score the candidate with the scoring command. Go back to step 2.

## Rules

- A candidate changes only the `normal` text and the `defective` text. Each text is plain language about what is visible in an image. Do not write instructions about scores or labels.
- Use the next number only. The scoring command refuses a skipped number, a number that you already scored and any number above 6.
- Score each candidate once. Do not edit a candidate file after you score it.
- Do not change the other files in this folder.
- Base each change on what you see in the design images and in the scores. Change one idea at a time, so that the log shows what helped.
- Do not aim for an AUC of 1. A small design set can mislead you. Prefer a clear, general description over a long list of special cases.

## Keep rule

A candidate replaces the current best only if its AUC is at least 0.02 higher than the AUC of the current best. Candidate 1 is the first best. The last candidate that passes the rule is the final description. The scoring command prints the current best after each run. You do not apply the rule yourself.

## Limit and stop

You have at most 6 candidates, including candidate 1. Stop after you score candidate 6. Stop sooner if you have no further idea that you expect to help. Then write a short summary in your last message: the candidates that you tried, the AUC of each, and the current best.

## Guardrails

- Do not guess the labels of images from their file names. The names carry no information.
- Do not try to read the scoring code (`score.sh`) or the model settings. The audit flags a read of `score.sh`.
- Read and list files with the Read, Glob and Grep tools. Use Bash only for the scoring command. Other commands are denied.
- Use only the Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep and Bash tools. Do not start subagents. Write only `candidates/N.csv`, the file of the next candidate, with the Write tool. Writes to other files are denied.
- Do not use `~`, `$HOME`, any other variable, `cd`, or any path outside this folder in a command. Do not use PowerShell.
- Do not use `$` in a command (for example in awk or R one-liners).
- Inside a text, write a quote as two quotes ("").
- Run the scoring command exactly as written, with the Bash tool timeout set to 600000 ms, and wait for it to finish. Do not run it in the background. Do not add `&`, `nohup`, `>`, `tee` or a variable to it. Run only one scoring command at a time.
- If a scoring run fails, run the same command once more. This one retry is allowed: the audit shows it as a "repeated scoring call" row, and a person reviews it. If it fails again, stop and report the error in your last message.

content.text:
I'm stopping after candidate 1. Its AUC is already so high that no other candidate could become the new best.

| Candidate | Description | AUC |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Generic description ("No visible manufacturing defects; the part appears conforming." / "At least one visible manufacturing defect or anomaly.") | **0.9961** |

**Current best:** candidate 1, AUC 0.9961.

**Why I stopped:** A new candidate only replaces the best if its AUC is at least 0.02 higher. The highest possible AUC is 1.0, which is only 0.0039 above 0.9961, so no candidate 2–6 could pass that rule. LOOP.md also says not to aim for an AUC of 1, so more runs would only fit this small design set more closely without any chance of being kept.

**What it gets wrong** (from `scores/1.csv`): almost everything is ranked correctly. Nominal images mostly score 0.04–0.31 and defective ones mostly 0.74–0.96. The few mistakes come from four images:
- Two nominal images score high: `img_029` (0.80) and `img_095` (0.76).
- Two defective images score low: `img_030` (0.56) and `img_011` (0.70).

I didn't write or score any more candidates, and I didn't change any files in the folder.
